network.overall_strategy: Valine is treated as a skeleton-limited target. The network therefore centers the two experimentally strongest late-stage solutions: classical Strecker chemistry on isobutyraldehyde and direct conversion of alpha-ketoisovaleric acid by mineral/metal-mediated reductive amination or by Bucherer-Bergs hydantoin chemistry. Upstream branched-skeleton supply is kept explicit and evidence-weighted: a surface acetone-to-isobutyraldehyde cyanosulfidic sequence is included because Patel-type chemistry reaches the valine aminonitrile branch, while a CO/H2 Fe-Ni route is retained only as a flagged hydrothermal alternative. Alpha-ketoisovaleric acid itself is left as a supplied hub intermediate because the literature identifies its abiotic synthesis as unresolved. Known competing sinks to pantoate and alpha-hydroxyisovalerate are acknowledged in the literature but not expanded here so the network remains within the requested size cap.

reactions.name: Acetone cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: cyanide-rich evaporitic or geothermal pool; cyanohydrin capture favored during concentration and limited dilution

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds nucleophilically to the ketone carbonyl and the alkoxide is protonated to give the tertiary cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: This is the entry step of the Patel/Sutherland branched-valine branch and is straightforward cyanohydrin chemistry under cyanide-bearing surface conditions (Patel et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2023). It is retained because it is one of the few experimentally grounded ways to begin assembling the branched valine skeleton from simple carbonyl chemistry.

reactions.name: Cyanosulfidic conversion of acetone cyanohydrin to isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: short-wave UV irradiation; HS-/H2S as stoichiometric reductant; staged delivery in shallow pools or streams

reactions.mechanism: The cyanohydrin is sulfurized through thioamide-like intermediates and then photoredox-driven deoxygenation and rearrangement deliver the aldehyde oxidation state.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. showed the acetone branch can be carried through sulfur chemistry and Cu photoredox to the valine aminonitrile level. This node is a mass-balanced summary of that staged sequence, keeping the required sulfide and UV explicit. The branch is experimentally important but geochemically contested because it needs localized sulfide, UV, and reagent staging (Patel et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2023; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: FTT-like CO hydrogenation to isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: subseafloor gas-water-mineral interface; rapid quenching needed to preserve aldehydes

reactions.mechanism: Surface-mediated carbonyl coupling and hydrogenation on reduced metal and mineral surfaces generate mixed C4 oxygenates.
reactions.reasoning: FTT-type CO/H2 chemistry on Fe-Ni surfaces is a chemically plausible but weakly supported alternative source of branched aldehydes. The cited literature reports amino-acid formation from CO/H2/NH3 over Fe-Ni catalysts but does not robustly establish isobutyraldehyde itself; this node is therefore explicitly speculative and included only as a contested upstream skeleton source (Yoshino et al., 1971; NASA TM X-62,411, 1975; Glavin et al., 2010; Elsila et al., 2021).

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis of valine aminonitrile from isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: evaporitic pool, aerosol film, or cyanide reservoir setting; ferrocyanide or Prussian Blue can buffer cyanide availability

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condenses with the aldehyde to an imine or iminium that is trapped by cyanide, giving the alpha-aminonitrile and releasing water overall.
reactions.reasoning: The Strecker end-game from isobutyraldehyde is one of the strongest prebiotic routes to valine or its aminonitrile precursor. Valine has been made in Strecker-style systems using ferrocyanide-based cyanide storage, and this chemistry also underlies the aqueous processing of spark-discharge aldehydes and HCN (Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013; Ring et al., 1972; Johnson et al., 2009). The major uncertainty lies upstream in making and preserving isobutyraldehyde.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of valine aminonitrile to valine

conditions.other: prolonged hydration, geothermal warming, or repeated wet-dry and rehydration cycles

reactions.mechanism: Stepwise nitrile hydration and hydrolysis convert the aminonitrile to the amino acid; ammonia is the net coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis is the standard completion step of Strecker chemistry and converts the experimentally accessible valine aminonitrile into free valine under sustained aqueous heating. It is the natural end of both classical Strecker routes and the Patel/Sutherland valine branch (Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Ni-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovaleric acid

conditions.other: pH about 8; mineral-interface aqueous system; laboratory proof used as mild analog for H2-fed prebiotic mineral chemistry

reactions.mechanism: The ketoacid forms an imine with ammonia and the imine is hydrogenated on nickel, competing with but not eliminating ketoacid reduction.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. directly demonstrated alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine under H2 and ammonia on Ni catalysts, and reported no conversion without catalyst. This is one of the most secure valine-specific end-games, but it deliberately leaves the prebiotic origin of alpha-ketoisovaleric acid unresolved because the literature does not yet solve that problem (Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Pd/C-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovaleric acid

conditions.other: pH about 8; high amino-acid selectivity relative to hydroxy-acid side products

reactions.mechanism: Pd-catalyzed imine hydrogenation efficiently channels the ketoacid toward the amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Pd/C gave the highest amino-acid selectivity in the alpha-ketoacid reductive amination study of Kaur et al., including the alpha-KIV to valine conversion. Palladium is geochemically rarer than Ni, so this node is best viewed as an experimentally strong benchmark rather than the most abundant natural catalyst (Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Fe-Ni meteorite-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovaleric acid

conditions.other: pH about 8; heterogeneous metal grains as catalytic interfaces

reactions.mechanism: Imine formation is followed by hydrogen transfer on meteoritic Fe-Ni metal surfaces.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. showed that ground Aletai iron meteorite catalyzes reductive amination of biological alpha-ketoacids, including alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine. This makes the end-game geochemically attractive because Fe-Ni metal is plausible in localized meteoritic or serpentinization-linked settings (Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: FeS/H2S-mediated reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovaleric acid

conditions.other: sulfide-rich vent wall or subseafloor pore; pH near the NH4+/NH3 transition; coupling to pyrite-forming chemistry

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine with the ketoacid and Fe-S redox chemistry drives reduction while sulfide is oxidized to elemental sulfur overall.
reactions.reasoning: FeS/H2S systems were reported to promote reductive amination of alpha-oxo acids in metabolism-first experiments, with electron flow coupled to sulfide and pyrite chemistry. Alpha-ketoisovalerate was not the headline substrate in those papers, so this valine-specific node is weaker than the Ni, Pd, and meteorite routes but remains chemically grounded in the demonstrated Fe-S reaction class (Hafenbradl et al., 1995; Huber and Wachtershauser, 2003).

reactions.name: Fe(OH)2-mediated reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovaleric acid

conditions.other: alkaline Fe2+-rich mineral interface; high ammonia favored; net written against environmental H2

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide-rich Fe(II) surfaces assist imine formation and reduction to the amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Fresh Fe(OH)2 was reported to promote reductive amination of alpha-keto acids in the Fe(II)-based studies of Huber and Wachtershauser, and iron oxyhydroxide systems later showed analogous amino-acid formation from pyruvate. The original Fe(OH)2 experiments used Fe(II)-rich precipitates as the immediate electron source; the present balanced node is written against environmental H2 to keep the network comparable, so it is more speculative than the direct Ni, Pd, and meteorite demonstrations (Huber and Wachtershauser, 2003; Barge et al., 2019).

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs formation of valine hydantoin from alpha-ketoisovaleric acid
reactions.mechanism: Cyanide and ammonia add to the ketoacid and cyclize under carbonate-buffered aqueous conditions to the hydantoin.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. showed that alpha-ketoacids undergo Bucherer-Bergs chemistry efficiently in bicarbonate buffer, forming hydantoins that can later hydrolyze to amino acids. Applying that reaction class to alpha-ketoisovaleric acid is chemically well motivated, although the literature still leaves alpha-KIV supply unresolved and the broader cyanide-availability critique remains (Pulletikurti et al., 2022; Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of valine hydantoin to valine

conditions.other: geothermal heating-cooling cycles or prolonged warm-pool hydrolysis

reactions.mechanism: Ring opening and hydrolysis of the hydantoin release the amino acid together with ammonia and carbon dioxide.
reactions.reasoning: Hydantoin hydrolysis is the slower completion step of the Bucherer-Bergs route and was demonstrated at elevated temperature in the alpha-ketoacid study of Pulletikurti et al. This provides a conceptually distinct late-stage route to valine from the same alpha-keto hub (Pulletikurti et al., 2022).

pathways.name: Acetone cyanosulfidic-Strecker pathway
pathways.description: Acetone is trapped as its cyanohydrin, converted by sulfide, copper, and UV chemistry to isobutyraldehyde, then carried through Strecker chemistry and hydrolysis to valine. This is the most experimentally elaborated surface branch to a valine precursor, though staging and sulfide supply are debated.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin reservoir completion pathway
pathways.description: If acetone cyanohydrin is already accumulated from upstream cyanide chemistry, only the sulfide-driven conversion and Strecker finishing steps are needed to reach valine.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal CO-to-Strecker pathway
pathways.description: A speculative Fe-Ni carbon monoxide hydrogenation branch supplies isobutyraldehyde, which after quenching and transfer into a cyanide-rich surface pool enters the experimentally strong Strecker end-game.

pathways.name: Direct Strecker end-game from isobutyraldehyde
pathways.description: Any prior source of isobutyraldehyde, including routes not expanded here, can feed the classical late-stage valine aminonitrile and hydrolysis sequence.

pathways.name: Nickel-catalyzed alpha-KIV reductive amination
pathways.description: Assuming alpha-ketoisovaleric acid is available, nickel under H2 and ammonia gives the best-studied direct catalytic conversion to valine.

pathways.name: Pd/C-catalyzed alpha-KIV reductive amination
pathways.description: Assuming alpha-ketoisovaleric acid is available, Pd/C carries out the same end-game with especially high amino-acid selectivity.

pathways.name: Meteoritic Fe-Ni alpha-KIV reductive amination
pathways.description: Assuming alpha-ketoisovaleric acid is available, ground Fe-Ni meteorite substitutes for synthetic catalysts and still converts the ketoacid directly to valine.

pathways.name: FeS/H2S alpha-KIV reductive amination
pathways.description: In a sulfur-rich vent-like setting, FeS and sulfide provide a metabolism-first style route from alpha-ketoisovaleric acid to valine; the reaction class is supported, but valine-specific evidence is less direct than for Ni or Pd.

pathways.name: Fe(OH)2 alpha-KIV reductive amination
pathways.description: Fresh Fe(OH)2 offers an Fe2+-rich mineral-interface alternative to Ni and Pd for the final amination step, again assuming alpha-ketoisovaleric acid is available.

pathways.name: Bucherer-Bergs hydantoin pathway
pathways.description: Alpha-ketoisovaleric acid can also reach valine through cyanide and ammonia capture as valine hydantoin, followed by warm aqueous hydrolysis. This route is chemically distinct from direct reductive amination but inherits the same alpha-KIV bottleneck.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Conceptually aligns with Patel-type cyanosulfidic access to the valine aminonitrile branch, but rxn_002 is too compressed to count as a well-specified single reaction. The literature route needs staged H2S/HS-, Cu photoredox and 254 nm UV; as written, rxn_002 is only balanced with 2 H2S. rxn_005 is only balanced with 2 H2O and likely needs stronger hydrolysis conditions. Good route conceptually, but under-specified chemically.
suggestions: Split rxn_002 into explicit thioamide and photoreduction steps or route directly to the Patel-type aminonitrile branch.
Add Cu(I)/Cu(II), HS-/H2S and 254 nm UV conditions and correct rxn_002 to use 2 H2S.
Annotate rxn_005 with 2 H2O and explicit hydrolysis conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Reasonable if acetone cyanohydrin is treated as stored reservoir material, but the key cyanosulfidic reduction/deoxygenation is still compressed into rxn_002. rxn_002 needs 2 H2S for balance and should include Cu/UV/HS- conditions or be split into explicit substeps; rxn_005 needs 2 H2O. Downstream Strecker chemistry is solid.
suggestions: Split rxn_002 into explicit cyanosulfidic substeps or route directly to valine aminonitrile.
Add Cu photoredox, HS-/H2S and 254 nm UV conditions and correct rxn_002 to use 2 H2S.
Annotate rxn_005 with 2 H2O and realistic hydrolysis conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Strecker end-game is credible, but rxn_003 is a very speculative shortcut: direct selective CO/H2 to isobutyraldehyde is not robustly established and the reaction needs explicit Fe-Ni-like catalysis and 4 CO + 7 H2 stoichiometry. The pathway also shifts from Hydrothermal to Surface without explaining transfer and concentration of isobutyraldehyde. Overall this branch is weak.
suggestions: Replace rxn_003 with a better-supported upstream source of isobutyraldehyde or flag it as highly speculative.
Specify catalyst and correct stoichiometry for rxn_003 to 4 CO + 7 H2 -> C4H8O + 3 H2O.
Justify hydrothermal-to-surface transfer and concentration of isobutyraldehyde.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strongest pathway in the network. Classical Strecker chemistry on isobutyraldehyde is well supported by the literature and the two-step logic is coherent. The main correction is rxn_005, which balances only as aminonitrile + 2 H2O -> valine + NH3 and generally needs hotter or longer hydrolysis than the network states.
suggestions: Correct rxn_005 stoichiometry to include 2 H2O.
Specify hydrolysis conditions such as heating, pH cycling or mineral assistance.
Add an upstream defended source of isobutyraldehyde and relevant competing sinks if a more complete route is desired.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Direct literature support exists for Ni-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-KIV to valine, so the chemistry is strong. However, the environment label Biochemical is inaccurate for an abiotic metal-catalyzed process, the catalyst named is a laboratory Ni/SiO2-Al2O3 material rather than a defended natural mineral, and the known alpha-hydroxyisovalerate side product is not represented. Best treated as a conditional late-stage route from supplied alpha-KIV.
suggestions: Relabel the environment as abiotic aqueous or mineral catalysis rather than Biochemical.
Use a geochemically defended Ni phase or explicitly justify Ni/SiO2-Al2O3 as an analog.
Add alpha-hydroxyisovalerate as a competing product and provide or justify alpha-KIV supply.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: As a laboratory transformation this is excellent, but as a prebiotic pathway it is weak. Pd/C is not a realistic environmental catalyst, the Biochemical label is inconsistent, and alpha-KIV is still externally supplied. This is best viewed as benchmark chemistry rather than a defended natural pathway.
suggestions: Frame Pd/C explicitly as a laboratory benchmark, not a plausible prebiotic catalyst.
If prebiotic realism is intended, replace Pd/C with Fe-Ni or Ni-bearing natural phases.
Provide or justify alpha-KIV supply.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest alpha-KIV branch. Kaur et al. directly support Fe-Ni meteorite-catalyzed reductive amination to valine, and the catalyst is more geochemically defensible than Pd/C or supported Ni. Remaining issues are the inaccurate Biochemical label, lack of explicit H2 and pH conditions, and the unresolved source of alpha-KIV.
suggestions: Relabel the environment as meteoritic metal-catalyzed aqueous chemistry rather than Biochemical.
Add the reported H2 pressure, pH 8 aqueous medium and expected hydroxy-acid competition.
Provide or justify alpha-KIV supply.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrothermal FeS/H2S chemistry is environmentally plausible and older iron-sulfur literature supports analogous ketoacid aminations, but this exact alpha-KIV to valine conversion is less directly evidenced than the Ni, Pd or meteorite cases. Plausible as an analog branch, but not yet as strong as the best-supported end-games.
suggestions: Specify fresh FeS, H2S/HS-, pH and ammonia loading explicitly.
Note that this branch is analogy-supported unless a valine-specific alpha-KIV citation is added.
Add alpha-hydroxyisovalerate as a competing sink if selectivity matters.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This branch is weakly specified. Fe(OH)2 or green-rust-like minerals can mediate analogous ketoacid amination chemistry, but the pathway is mislabeled Biochemical and the reaction stoichiometry uses H2 even though the cited Fe(II)/hydroxide literature often relies on Fe(II) as the reductant. Valine from alpha-KIV is therefore only analogy-supported here.
suggestions: Relabel the environment to mineral or aqueous rather than Biochemical.
Clarify whether Fe(OH)2, green rust or another Fe(II) hydroxide phase is intended and how reduction is driven.
Do not use H2 as the sole reductant unless a matching valine-specific precedent is cited.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Bucherer-Bergs logic is coherent and literature-supported in general for alpha-ketoacids, but the conditions are incomplete. rxn_011 should specify bicarbonate or CO2 buffering, and rxn_012 is only balanced with 2 H2O and usually requires heated hydrolysis. The Biochemical label is again misleading for an abiotic cyanide and hydantoin sequence.
suggestions: Add bicarbonate or CO2 buffering explicitly to rxn_011 conditions.
Correct rxn_012 to include 2 H2O and specify heated hydrolysis.
Relabel the environment away from Biochemical and provide or justify alpha-KIV supply.

evaluation.network_feedback: Connected, literature-aware network with 15 molecules and 12 reactions; there are no isolated subgraphs and the balance check reports no unbalanced reactions. Four reactions still need explicit stoichiometric coefficients: rxn_002 = C4H7NO + 2 H2S -> C4H8O + NH3 + 2 S, rxn_003 = 4 CO + 7 H2 -> C4H8O + 3 H2O, rxn_005 = C5H10N2 + 2 H2O -> C5H11NO2 + NH3, and rxn_012 = C6H10N2O2 + 2 H2O -> C5H11NO2 + NH3 + CO2. The network aligns well with the literature by centering the two strongest valine end-games, Strecker chemistry from isobutyraldehyde and alpha-KIV conversion by reductive amination or Bucherer-Bergs chemistry, and by explicitly acknowledging that alpha-KIV synthesis is unresolved. The main weaknesses are that rxn_002 compresses the Patel-style cyanosulfidic sequence and omits Cu photoredox, 254 nm UV and HS- staging, rxn_003 is a very speculative FTT-like shortcut to a specific branched aldehyde, and several reactions are mislabeled Biochemical even though they are abiotic mineral or metal chemistry. Competing sinks such as alpha-hydroxyisovalerate and pantoate or pantolactone are acknowledged but not represented. Best-supported route here is P4, with P7 the strongest alpha-KIV branch. Overall this is a good, evidence-weighted network, but it is not approval-ready under the >= 0.9 threshold.
